Fallacy

/FAL-uh-see/ — stress on first syllable, rhymes with gallery · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A fallacy is a widely believed idea that is actually false or based on flawed reasoning.

The idea that lightning never strikes twice is a well-known fallacy.

Worked Example

Most medieval people believed that the sun orbited the earth, accepting an astronomical fallacy that dominated thought for centuries.

Fallacy is more precise than 'mistake' because it emphasizes a belief that is widely accepted despite being false or based on faulty reasoning. A mistake is personal error; a fallacy is deeply embedded in common (but wrong) knowledge.

How Fallacy Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

myth

myth: a widely shared belief that isn't true

misconception

misconception: a mistaken understanding of how something works

falsehood

falsehood: a statement that is simply not true

Antonyms

fact

fact: something proven true by real evidence

truth

truth: what actually happened or is real

How Strong Is It? — mistake → misconception → delusion → fallacy

mistake vs. fallacy

mistake vs. fallacy: A mistake is much weaker than a fallacy; a mistake is a single slip anyone can make, while a fallacy is a flawed idea that whole crowds keep believing.

misconception vs. fallacy

misconception vs. fallacy: A misconception is slightly weaker than a fallacy: a misconception is one person's mixed-up understanding, while a fallacy is false reasoning so widespread it can pass for common sense.

delusion vs. fallacy

delusion vs. fallacy: A delusion is stronger than a fallacy — a fallacy is a false belief you can be argued out of, but a delusion grips someone's mind even when the evidence against it is undeniable.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — fall-

Root — fall-: to deceive, trip up (Latin)

Suffix — -acy

Suffix — -acy: state or quality (noun-forming) (Latin via Old French)

Put it together

Put it together: The Latin root fall- means 'to deceive or trip up,' and the suffix -acy turns it into a noun naming a state or quality. A fallacy is literally a 'deceiving thing' — an idea that trips up your reasoning because it is false.

Use the root in a new word: infallible

Use the root in a new word: infallible: The referee acted as if he were infallible — unable to be deceived or to make an error — the same Latin root fall-, 'to deceive,' found in fallacy.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / neutral

Fallacy is the precise word when you want to name a widespread false belief that many people accept despite weak reasoning. For a single person's false belief, use 'misconception.' For a simple untruth, 'false' or 'lie' works better.
